newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-RIVALS CONCEDE MASTERS VICTORY TO WOODS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-RIVALS CONCEDE MASTERS VICTORY TO WOODS.

text.p: Tiger Woods's rivals all agreed Saturday that the 21-year-old sensation had turned the Masters into one heck of a race for second place.

"It's not humanly possible that Tiger Woods is going to lose this tournament. No way," said Briton Colin Montgomerie, who started the third round in second place, three shots behind Woods, and finished 12 strokes behind.
"He is like a boy amongst men and showing the men how to play," said 47-year-old Tom Watson, who shot 69 Saturday to stand tied for fourth place, 11 strokes back of Woods.
"He can make nine bogeys tomorrow and still be in position to win the tournament."
Woods fired a flawless seven-under-par 65 Saturday -- the second successive day he posted the best score in the field -- to leave his pursuers in the dust.

Woods will be paired Sunday with Italy's Costantino Rocca, who birdied the 18th to reach six under par and move into second place -- a massive nine shots away from Woods's Masters record-tying 54-hole total of 15-under-par 201.
"Catch Tiger? Maybe if I play nine holes (instead of 18) -- under par, too," Rocca joked.

Woods's nine-shot lead going into the final round is a Masters record. It is even more impressive considering the young American staggered to a four-over-par start of 40 on his opening front nine Thursday.

Woods, a three-time U.S. Amateur champion playing in his first Masters as a professional, has gone an amazing 19 under par over 45 holes since. He needs 69 to eclipse the Masters scoring mark of 271 shared by Jack Nicklaus and Raymond Floyd.
Paul Stankowski was alone in third place at five-under 211, 10 shots off the astonishing pace set by Woods.
"If I can make five, six, seven birdies early like on...like on the first three holes, I might have a chance," cracked Stankowski.

Jeff Sluman, the 1988 PGA champion who was tied for sixth, a dozen shots back, suggested there would have been an exciting Masters title chase had Woods continued his studies at Stanford rather than turn professional.
"I wish he had stayed in school and gotten his PHD," joked Sluman.
It should be noted that just last year the Masters produced an incredible turnabout finish after Greg Norman took a six-shot lead over Nick Faldo into the final round.
Faldo shot 67 and Norman, who has a history of disappointing finishes in majors, staggered to a 78 for an 11-shot swing in the biggest collapse in major championship golf.
Montgomerie said there was no chance of that happening during Masters Sunday this year.
"Faldo is not laying in second place for starts," said Montgomerie, of the three-time Masters winner. "And Greg Norman is not Tiger Woods."
